input:
This passage reports the results of a pilot-scale test of an amine absorption unit treating gas from a cement kiln, a source whose gas composition and dust loading might be expected to raise questions about how well a capture unit performs outside a cleaner test setting. The unit was operated over 90 days at a rate of 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, and over that period it captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, which can be regarded as a substantial capture fraction sustained over a test of meaningful length rather than a brief demonstration. The associated utility and solvent figures were also recorded: steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured, both of which are relevant to the operating cost of the process at larger scale. It should nevertheless be kept in mind that the test has a clear limit. Beyond the test period, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, so questions about longer-term solvent behaviour, and about any gradual change in performance that dust exposure might bring about, cannot be answered from these results and would require a longer campaign in which the solvent itself was monitored as the exposure accumulated.

Operating on gas drawn from an actual cement kiln, rather than on a prepared gas of fixed composition, also exposes the unit to the variation of a real source, and the results carry that exposure with them. Kiln operation changes as raw feed and burning conditions change, and the gas reaching the unit reflects those changes in its dust burden and in the load placed on the solvent. A capture fraction held across such variation, over the full duration of the test, is in this respect a stronger result than the same fraction held on a steady prepared gas for a short run, and the solvent loss figure, recorded across the whole campaign, likewise reflects contact with the real gas rather than with a clean substitute.

An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Capture at that fraction was sustained over the full test period, not held for a brief demonstration. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Steam demand and solvent loss set much of the operating cost of the process at larger scale, and both were recorded on the same basis, per tonne captured. The test period sets the limit of the results. Beyond the test period, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Longer-term solvent behaviour, and any gradual change in performance under continued dust exposure, cannot be read from the pilot results. A longer campaign, with the solvent monitored as exposure accumulates, is the measurement that would settle the question. The pilot results support the capture fraction, the steam demand, and the solvent loss at the stated rate and duration. Claims about solvent life under kiln dust stand outside the pilot results.

Gas drawn from an actual cement kiln varies as raw feed and burning conditions change. Dust burden and the load placed on the solvent vary with the kiln. A capture fraction held across that variation, over the full test period, is a stronger result than the same fraction held briefly on a prepared gas of fixed composition. The solvent loss figure belongs to the same picture. Solvent loss was recorded across the whole campaign, under contact with the real gas. A clean substitute gas would give a loss figure for different conditions. Performance figures from the pilot are therefore figures for kiln gas as fired, with its variation included. The figures are not figures for a smoothed feed, and a design that treats the kiln gas as steady takes on a variation the pilot results do not support.
